opus-5.5.text:
I think the most fundamental difference comes down to data and to the nature of the world each one deals with.

Internet AI lives in a world of information. Text, images, video: all of this has already been produced by humanity and accumulated over decades online. So when we train a large language model, we're essentially compressing the knowledge that's already sitting there. The data is massive, it's relatively cheap to get, and the outputs are also information. You generate a sentence or an image, and if it's a bit wrong, the cost is usually low. You can just regenerate it.

Embodied AI has to act in the physical world, and that changes everything. First, there's no internet of robot data. Nobody has been uploading trillions of tokens of "how a hand grasps a cup under different lighting, with different friction, from different angles." That data basically doesn't exist at scale, so we have to create it, whether through teleoperation, simulation, or synthetic data. I personally believe very strongly in simulation and synthetic data. Real-world teleoperation alone is just too slow and too expensive to reach the scale a foundation model needs.

Second, the physical world is a closed loop. When a robot acts, the world changes, and the next observation depends on what it just did. Errors compound. A language model making a small mistake in one token is mostly fine. A robot slightly misjudging a grasp might drop the object, and now it's in a completely different state it may never have seen before. So you need robustness, real-time feedback, and generalization in a way internet AI mostly doesn't have to worry about.

Third, there's the hardware and the body itself. Internet AI runs on GPUs in a data center, and the "body" is uniform. In embodied AI, the morphology matters: the hands, the sensors, the dynamics. Intelligence is tied to the body, and the body is still evolving rapidly. That makes standardization much harder.

So I'd summarize it this way: internet AI is about understanding and generating information from data humanity already has, while embodied AI has to generate its own data and close the loop between perception, decision, and physical action. That's why I think embodied AI is still at a much earlier stage. It's maybe at a pre-GPT moment, where the key question is still how to get enough high-quality data to unlock generalization.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots acting in a changing physical world and says intelligence is tied to the body, but it does not clearly identify body–environment interaction as the source of embodied AI’s intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response says simulation can help create robot data, but does not state that interaction in a physics-based simulator supplies experience from which embodied AI learns.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core distinction comes down to what the system has to deal with: information versus the physical world.

Internet AI, the large language models and the recommendation systems and so on, lives entirely in the space of data that humans have already produced. Text, images, video, code. That data is abundant, it is already digitized, and crucially it is already a kind of compressed representation of human knowledge. So the problem is mostly about scale and about learning the structure that is already there. You feed it enough, and it gets very good at predicting and generating within that space. The world it operates in is, in a sense, closed and clean.

Embodied AI is different in a fundamental way. A robot has to perceive the physical world, reason about it, and then act in it, and its actions change the state of the world, which it then has to perceive again. That loop is where everything gets hard. First, there is no internet-scale dataset of robot interaction. Nobody has been recording billions of hours of grasping cups and opening drawers with labeled actions. The data has to be collected, or simulated, or somehow bootstrapped, and it is expensive. Second, the physical world is continuous and governed by physics. Contact, friction, deformation, occlusion. A language model can be approximately right and still be useful. A robot that is approximately right about where the handle is drops the cup. Third, there is generalization. Internet AI generalizes across text because text is text. Embodied AI has to generalize across objects it has never seen, environments with different lighting and clutter, and robot bodies with different kinematics. The variance is enormous.

So I would say internet AI is primarily a problem of understanding, and embodied AI adds the problem of interaction under physical constraints with scarce data. The good news is that the two are starting to connect. The semantic understanding and common sense that come out of large models give robots a kind of prior about the world that we never had before. The open question, and the one I spend most of my time on, is how to combine that high-level understanding with the low-level, physically grounded skills that actually let a machine manipulate things reliably. That bridge, from perception to action, is really what embodied AI is about.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots perceiving and acting in the physical world, but does not identify body–environment interaction as the source of embodied AI’s intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says data may be simulated, but does not state that interaction in a physics-based simulator supplies experience for embodied AI to learn from.

astra-6.text:
I think the core distinction is whether the AI must act in the physical world. Internet AI primarily operates on digital information: it takes in text, images, or video and produces an answer or some digital output. Embodied AI has to connect perception to action. It needs to understand its surroundings, decide what to do, act, and then observe how the world changes.

That creates a different kind of challenge. Imagine asking a robot to pick up a cup. Recognizing the cup is only the beginning. The robot has to judge where to grasp it, how much force to use, and whether it’s slipping, then adjust as it moves. Its actions change what it perceives next.

So I’d emphasize that continuous loop of perception, action, and feedback. Physical environments are uncertain, and mistakes have real consequences. Intelligence has to work under those conditions, rather than stopping at a plausible answer.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a physics-based simulator or simulator-supplied learning experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core distinction is whether the AI has to close the loop with the physical world. Internet AI mainly operates on digital information: it takes in text, images, or video and produces an answer. Embodied AI has to perceive its surroundings, take an action, and then understand how that action changed the world.

That makes the problem quite different. If a robot picks up a cup, recognizing the cup is only the beginning. It also needs to work out where to grasp it, how much force to apply, and how to adjust if the cup slips. Its actions affect what it observes next, so perception, decision-making, and control have to work together.

And the physical world imposes real constraints. Data is harder to collect, mistakes can damage things, and the same action can have different outcomes in different situations. So the key challenge is turning knowledge into reliable action under uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied AI closes the loop with the physical world and that actions change what it observes next. It does not identify body-environment interaction as the source of embodied AI’s intelligence.
